walkthroughs.body_html:
When a wave hits a barrier it can reflect — bounce back.

The angle of incidence (measured from the normal, not the surface) equals the angle of reflection. Always from the normal!

You see this with mirrors, echoes from a wall, and straight wavefronts bouncing off a barrier in a ripple tank.

When a wave crosses into a new medium it can change speed. If it hits the boundary at an angle, this change of speed makes it bend — that's refraction.

Water waves slow down when they cross from deep to shallow water in a ripple tank. As they slow, their wavelength gets shorter but their frequency stays the same.

A wavefront is a line joining bits of the wave that are doing the same thing at the same time — like the crest of a single ripple.

Straight wavefronts in deep water turn at a boundary and become straight wavefronts in shallow water travelling in a new direction.

In an exam, draw the wavefronts closer together where the wave is slower. 📏

Frequency decreases, speed stays the same
